raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure caused by left ventricular systolic dysfunction, usually during the last month of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, when no alternative cause is found [1]. Contemporary definitions emphasize diagnosis late in pregnancy or postpartum, exclusion of other causes, and typically left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% [2]. Although uncommon, PPCM is a major cause of maternal morbidity and mortality because it affects young women, may progress rapidly to cardiogenic shock, and has implications for subsequent pregnancies [3-5].

Incidence varies markedly by geography and ascertainment. Population studies from the United States suggest approximately 1 case per 1000–4000 live births, with rising recognition over time and disproportionate burden among Black women [6-8]. Much higher rates have been reported in Haiti and parts of sub-Saharan Africa, reflecting genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, nutritional status, access to care, and differences in case finding [9,10]. Risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, and African ancestry [11-13]. PPCM can present antepartum, but many cases are diagnosed in the early postpartum period, when normal pregnancy-related dyspnea, edema, and fatigue may delay recognition [11].

Pathobiology is multifactorial. Experimental and translational data support an anti-angiogenic milieu, particularly in pre-eclampsia and multiple gestation, in which soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and vascular endothelial growth factor imbalance may impair myocardial microvascular homeostasis [14]. A complementary mechanism involves oxidative stress and cathepsin D cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa fragment with anti-angiogenic, pro-apoptotic, and vasculotoxic effects [15]. MicroRNA-146a has been implicated as a downstream mediator and potential biomarker [16]. Inflammatory activation is common and may correlate with outcome [10]. Genetic predisposition is increasingly recognized: truncating variants in cardiomyopathy genes, especially TTN, overlap substantially with dilated cardiomyopathy, supporting a “two-hit” model in which pregnancy unmasks latent susceptibility [19,20]. Biomarker studies in prospective cohorts further link vascular and myocardial stress pathways to clinical phenotype [30].

Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion. Symptoms include exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, edema, palpitations, thromboembolism, or shock. Evaluation includes electrocardiography, natriuretic peptides, chest imaging when appropriate, and urgent transthoracic echocardiography to document LVEF, ventricular size, right ventricular function, valvular disease, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus. Differential diagnoses include pre-existing dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertensive heart disease, myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, ischemia or spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and sepsis-related cardiomyopathy. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is useful postpartum when myocarditis, infarction, thrombus, or scar characterization is uncertain. Endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for selected cases with unexplained fulminant heart failure, arrhythmias, conduction disease, or suspected specific myocarditis where results would change management [29]. Pregnancy heart-team care is recommended for severe disease or ongoing pregnancy [28].

Prognosis is heterogeneous. In the North American IPAC cohort, most women improved substantially, but recovery was less likely with lower presenting LVEF, larger left ventricular end-diastolic dimension, Black race, and later diagnosis [21]. South African and German cohorts similarly demonstrate that baseline ventricular dysfunction, right ventricular involvement, and delayed presentation predict persistent dysfunction or adverse events [22,23]. Recovery may occur beyond 6 months, so prolonged follow-up is important [24,25]. Nevertheless, PPCM may lead to recurrent hospitalization, ventricular arrhythmias, thromboembolism, durable mechanical circulatory support, transplantation, or death.

Management combines standard heart failure therapy with pregnancy and lactation safety. During pregnancy, loop diuretics, beta-blockers, hydralazine, nitrates, and digoxin may be used when indicated; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided until after delivery. Postpartum, guideline-directed medical therapy should be initiated and titrated. Anticoagulation is considered for LVEF ≤35%, atrial fibrillation, ventricular thrombus, bromocriptine use, or other thrombotic risk. Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin, improved recovery in small studies and is considered in moderate-to-severe PPCM with concurrent anticoagulation, although practice varies [17,18]. Wearable defibrillators may bridge early arrhythmic risk, while implantable cardioverter-defibrillator decisions are usually deferred until reassessment after recovery time.

Counseling about future pregnancy is essential. Persistent LV dysfunction strongly increases maternal risk and pregnancy is generally discouraged [26]. Even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur; shared decision-making should include baseline echocardiography, medication adjustment before conception, close surveillance during pregnancy and postpartum, and discussion of fetal and maternal risks [27]. Long-term care should not end with normalization of LVEF: relapse, genetic cardiomyopathy, and late deterioration justify continued cardiology follow-up, family history assessment, and consideration of genetic counseling in selected patients.
